claim: Catarrhine primates (Old World anthropoids) include two extant subclades: cercopithecoids (Old World monkeys) and hominoids (apes and humans).
source: Catarrhine primates (Old World anthropoids) include two extant subclades: cercopithecoids (Old World monkeys) and hominoids (apes and humans).
evidence: This is a statement of established taxonomic classification in primatology.

claim: Cercopithecoids and hominoids diverged during the late Oligocene (≥25 Ma) based on molecular and paleontological data.
source: Based on molecular (e.g., Springer et al., 2012) and paleontological (e.g., Harrison, 2013; Stevens et al., 2013) data, both groups diverged during the late Oligocene (≥25 Ma), but experienced very different evolutionary histories.
evidence: The claim cites specific studies (Springer et al., 2012; Harrison, 2013; Stevens et al., 2013) that provide molecular and paleontological evidence for the divergence time.

claim: Hominoids first radiated in the early Miocene of Africa.
source: Hominoids first radiated in the early Miocene of Africa (Harrison, 2010; Begun, 2013; Begun, 2015) and subsequently diversified into Eurasia during the middle and late Miocene (Alba, 2012; Begun, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Harrison, 2010; Begun, 2013; Begun, 2015).

claim: Hominoids subsequently diversified into Eurasia during the middle and late Miocene.
source: Hominoids first radiated in the early Miocene of Africa (Harrison, 2010; Begun, 2013; Begun, 2015) and subsequently diversified into Eurasia during the middle and late Miocene (Alba, 2012; Begun, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Alba, 2012; Begun, 2015).

claim: The diversity and geographic distribution of hominoids (humans excluded) was much greater during the Miocene than at present.
source: Their diversity and geographic distribution (humans excluded) was much greater during the Miocene than at present, being currently restricted to a few genera in southeastern Asia and Africa.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about past and present hominoid diversity, drawing on established paleontological and biogeographic knowledge.

claim: Extant hominoids are currently restricted to a few genera in southeastern Asia and Africa.
source: Their diversity and geographic distribution (humans excluded) was much greater during the Miocene than at present, being currently restricted to a few genera in southeastern Asia and Africa.
evidence: This is a statement about the current biogeographic distribution of hominoids, based on established knowledge.

claim: Extant cercopithecoid lineages started to diversify later than hominoids and experienced a major radiation during the late Miocene.
source: In contrast, extant cercopithecoid lineages started to diversify later and experienced a major radiation during the late Miocene (Jablonski and Frost, 2010), being currently much more diverse and widely distributed than hominoids in both Africa and Asia.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jablonski and Frost, 2010.

claim: Cercopithecoids are currently much more diverse and widely distributed than hominoids in both Africa and Asia.
source: In contrast, extant cercopithecoid lineages started to diversify later and experienced a major radiation during the late Miocene (Jablonski and Frost, 2010), being currently much more diverse and widely distributed than hominoids in both Africa and Asia.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about current diversity and distribution, based on established biogeographic knowledge.

claim: The decimated current diversity of hominoids, coupled with the fragmentary nature of their fossil record, abundant homoplasy, and the lack of known fossil hylobatids prior to the latest Miocene make it difficult to confidently infer the phylogenetic relationships of extinct hominoids.
source: The decimated current diversity of hominoids, coupled with the fragmentary nature of their fossil record, abundant homoplasy (e.g., Larson, 1998), and the lack of known fossil hylobatids prior to the latest Miocene (Harrison, 2016) make it difficult to confidently infer the phylogenetic relationships of extinct hominoids and thus reliably infer the morphotype of the last common ancestor (LCA) of various hominoid subclades.
evidence: The claim cites Larson, 1998 for homoplasy and Harrison, 2016 for the lack of fossil hylobatids, and draws on general knowledge about fossil record limitations.

claim: There is a lack of known fossil hylobatids prior to the latest Miocene.
source: The decimated current diversity of hominoids, coupled with the fragmentary nature of their fossil record, abundant homoplasy (e.g., Larson, 1998), and the lack of known fossil hylobatids prior to the latest Miocene (Harrison, 2016) make it difficult to confidently infer the phylogenetic relationships of extinct hominoids and thus reliably infer the morphotype of the last common ancestor (LCA) of various hominoid subclades.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Harrison, 2016.

claim: Putative stem hominoids from the early Miocene of Africa, such as the proconsulid Ekembo, lack most of the synapomorphies of crown hominoids.
source: For example, putative stem hominoids from the early Miocene of Africa (Begun, 2013; Begun, 2015), such as the proconsulid Ekembo, lack most of the synapomorphies of crown hominoids, such that some authors still contend that they might represent stem catarrhines instead (Harrison, 2010; Harrison, 2013).
evidence: The claim cites Begun, 2013 and Begun, 2015 for the stem hominoid interpretation, and Harrison, 2010 and Harrison, 2013 for the alternative stem catarrhine interpretation.

claim: Some authors contend that proconsulids like Ekembo might represent stem catarrhines instead of stem hominoids.
source: For example, putative stem hominoids from the early Miocene of Africa (Begun, 2013; Begun, 2015), such as the proconsulid Ekembo, lack most of the synapomorphies of crown hominoids, such that some authors still contend that they might represent stem catarrhines instead (Harrison, 2010; Harrison, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Harrison, 2010 and Harrison, 2013.

claim: The position of dendropithecids (e.g., Micropithecus) and other small-bodied catarrhines from the early to middle Miocene of Africa is uncertain.
source: Even more uncertain is the position of dendropithecids (e.g., Micropithecus) and other small-bodied catarrhines from the early to middle Miocene of Africa, which are generally interpreted as stem catarrhines (Harrison, 2010; Harrison, 2013) but might include stem hominoids as well (Alba et al., 2015; Begun, 2015).
evidence: The claim cites Harrison, 2010 and Harrison, 2013 for the stem catarrhine interpretation, and Alba et al., 2015 and Begun, 2015 for the alternative stem hominoid interpretation.

claim: Dendropithecids are generally interpreted as stem catarrhines but might include stem hominoids as well.
source: Even more uncertain is the position of dendropithecids (e.g., Micropithecus) and other small-bodied catarrhines from the early to middle Miocene of Africa, which are generally interpreted as stem catarrhines (Harrison, 2010; Harrison, 2013) but might include stem hominoids as well (Alba et al., 2015; Begun, 2015).
evidence: The claim cites Harrison, 2010 and Harrison, 2013 for the stem catarrhine interpretation, and Alba et al., 2015 and Begun, 2015 for the alternative stem hominoid interpretation.

claim: The European middle to late Miocene Pliobates has been recovered as a stem hominoid more derived than proconsulids.
source: The same controversy applies to the European middle to late Miocene Pliobates, recovered as a stem hominoid more derived than proconsulids (Alba et al., 2015) or alternatively as a member of the stem catarrhine pliopithecoid radiation (Nengo et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Alba et al., 2015.

claim: Pliobates has alternatively been interpreted as a member of the stem catarrhine pliopithecoid radiation.
source: The same controversy applies to the European middle to late Miocene Pliobates, recovered as a stem hominoid more derived than proconsulids (Alba et al., 2015) or alternatively as a member of the stem catarrhine pliopithecoid radiation (Nengo et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nengo et al., 2017.

claim: The late Miocene Oreopithecus from Italy has been variously considered a hominid or a stem hominoid.
source: This is best exemplified by the late Miocene Oreopithecus from Italy, variously considered a hominid (Moyà Solà and Köhler, 1997; Harrison and Rook, 1997) or a stem hominoid (Nengo et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim cites Moyà Solà and Köhler, 1997 and Harrison and Rook, 1997 for the hominid interpretation, and Nengo et al., 2017 for the stem hominoid interpretation.

claim: Most Asian Miocene apes have been classically considered pongines.
source: For example, most Asian forms have been classically considered pongines (Begun, 2013), but most recently the late Miocene Lufengpithecus from China has been reinterpreted as a stem hominid (Kelley and Gao, 2012; Begun, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Begun, 2013.

claim: The late Miocene Lufengpithecus from China has been reinterpreted as a stem hominid.
source: For example, most Asian forms have been classically considered pongines (Begun, 2013), but most recently the late Miocene Lufengpithecus from China has been reinterpreted as a stem hominid (Kelley and Gao, 2012; Begun, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kelley and Gao, 2012 and Begun, 2015.

claim: The middle to late Miocene European dryopithecines have been interpreted as either stem hominids or hominines.
source: Even more controversial is the position of the middle to late Miocene European dryopithecines, interpreted as either stem hominids (Alba, 2012; Alba et al., 2015) or hominines (Begun, 2013; Begun, 2015), and further controversies apply when trying to decipher the phylogenetic relationships among various members of this extinct group.
evidence: The claim cites Alba, 2012 and Alba et al., 2015 for the stem hominid interpretation, and Begun, 2013 and Begun, 2015 for the hominine interpretation.

claim: The recently described dryopithecine Danuvius from Germany has been used to argue that bipedal and suspensory adaptations characterized the last common ancestor of crown hominids.
source: For example, the recently described dryopithecine Danuvius from Germany has been used to argue that bipedal and suspensory adaptations characterized the last common ancestor of crown hominids (Böhme et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Böhme et al., 2019.

claim: The dryopithecine Pierolapithecus was orthograde but lacked adaptations to both bipedalism and suspension.
source: However, without a phylogenetic analysis supporting a more basal branching of Danuvius compared with the older dryopithecine Pierolapithecus (Moyà-Solà et al., 2004), which was orthograde but lacked adaptations to both bipedalism and suspension (Alba et al., 2010; Alba, 2012), the implications for the ancestral condition of the group remain moot.
evidence: The claim cites Moyà-Solà et al., 2004 for the description of Pierolapithecus, and Alba et al., 2010 and Alba, 2012 for the interpretation of its locomotor adaptations.

claim: Enamel proteome sequences have been recovered from the early Pleistocene (1.9 Ma) fossil pongine Gigantopithecus.
source: The recent recovery of enamel proteome sequences from the early Pleistocene (1.9 Ma) fossil pongine Gigantopithecus (Welker et al., 2019) offers some hope that molecular data will become available for Miocene apes sometime in the future.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Welker et al., 2019.

claim: Anatomical structures that develop early during development and are not remodeled thereafter (such as the enamel-dentine junction of teeth) represent the best candidates for morphological features not very prone to homoplasy.
source: Anatomical structures that develop early during development and are not remodeled thereafter (such as the enamel-dentine junction of teeth) represent the best candidates (Corruccini, 1987; Skinner et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Corruccini, 1987 and Skinner et al., 2008.

claim: The inner ear is a very promising anatomical area for phylogenetic reconstruction.
source: In this regard, the inner ear is also a very promising anatomical area (Spoor and Zonneveld, 1998; Spoor et al., 2003), even if thus far its phylogenetic implications have been mostly explored for fossil hominins only (Quam et al., 2016; Conde-Valverde et al., 2018; Ponce de León et al., 2018; Beaudet, 2019a; Beaudet et al., 2019b), while its application to fossil apes has been mainly devoted to locomotor inferences (David et al., 2010; Malinzak et al., 2012; Rook et al., 2004; Ryan et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim cites Spoor and Zonneveld, 1998 and Spoor et al., 2003 for the phylogenetic potential of the inner ear, and multiple other studies for its application to hominins and apes.

claim: The phylogenetic implications of the inner ear have been mostly explored for fossil hominins only.
source: In this regard, the inner ear is also a very promising anatomical area (Spoor and Zonneveld, 1998; Spoor et al., 2003), even if thus far its phylogenetic implications have been mostly explored for fossil hominins only (Quam et al., 2016; Conde-Valverde et al., 2018; Ponce de León et al., 2018; Beaudet, 2019a; Beaudet et al., 2019b), while its application to fossil apes has been mainly devoted to locomotor inferences (David et al., 2010; Malinzak et al., 2012; Rook et al., 2004; Ryan et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Quam et al., 2016; Conde-Valverde et al., 2018; Ponce de León et al., 2018; Beaudet, 2019a; Beaudet et al., 2019b.

claim: The application of inner ear analysis to fossil apes has been mainly devoted to locomotor inferences.
source: In this regard, the inner ear is also a very promising anatomical area (Spoor and Zonneveld, 1998; Spoor et al., 2003), even if thus far its phylogenetic implications have been mostly explored for fossil hominins only (Quam et al., 2016; Conde-Valverde et al., 2018; Ponce de León et al., 2018; Beaudet, 2019a; Beaudet et al., 2019b), while its application to fossil apes has been mainly devoted to locomotor inferences (David et al., 2010; Malinzak et al., 2012; Rook et al., 2004; Ryan et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to David et al., 2010; Malinzak et al., 2012; Rook et al., 2004; Ryan et al., 2012.

claim: The inner ear is housed in the highly mineralized petrosal bone, which is frequently preserved in the fossil record.
source: Housed in the highly mineralized petrosal bone, which is frequently preserved in the fossil record, the inner ear is composed of a series of endolymph-filled membranes (encased in the corresponding bony labyrinths), namely the cochlea or cochlear duct (involved in hearing) and the vestibular apparatus (devoted to balance and vision stability).
evidence: This is a statement about the anatomical location and preservation potential of the inner ear, based on established anatomical and taphonomic knowledge.

claim: The inner ear is composed of a series of endolymph-filled membranes, namely the cochlea or cochlear duct (involved in hearing) and the vestibular apparatus (devoted to balance and vision stability).
source: Housed in the highly mineralized petrosal bone, which is frequently preserved in the fossil record, the inner ear is composed of a series of endolymph-filled membranes (encased in the corresponding bony labyrinths), namely the cochlea or cochlear duct (involved in hearing) and the vestibular apparatus (devoted to balance and vision stability).
evidence: This is a statement about the anatomical composition and function of the inner ear, based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The vestibule consists of three (anterior, posterior, and lateral) semicircular canals (SCs) and two macular organs (utricle and saccule).
source: The vestibule consists of three (anterior, posterior, and lateral) semicircular canals (SCs) and two macular organs (utricle and saccule).
evidence: This is a statement about the anatomical composition of the vestibule, based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The approximately orthogonal SCs sense angular accelerations and decelerations of the head.
source: The approximately orthogonal SCs sense angular accelerations and decelerations of the head, while the maculae perceive linear accelerations and thus provide gravity reference (Spoor and Zonneveld, 1998; Rabbitt et al., 2004; Johnson Chacko et al., 2018; Cheung and Ercoline, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Spoor and Zonneveld, 1998; Rabbitt et al., 2004; Johnson Chacko et al., 2018; Cheung and Ercoline, 2018.

claim: The maculae perceive linear accelerations and thus provide gravity reference.
source: The approximately orthogonal SCs sense angular accelerations and decelerations of the head, while the maculae perceive linear accelerations and thus provide gravity reference (Spoor and Zonneveld, 1998; Rabbitt et al., 2004; Johnson Chacko et al., 2018; Cheung and Ercoline, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Spoor and Zonneveld, 1998; Rabbitt et al., 2004; Johnson Chacko et al., 2018; Cheung and Ercoline, 2018.

claim: Differences in the relative size and morphology of the SCs have been correlated with locomotor agility.
source: Differences in the relative size and morphology of the SCs have been correlated with locomotor agility (Spoor et al., 1994; Spoor et al., 2007; Walker et al., 2008; Silcox et al., 2009; Ryan et al., 2012; Perier et al., 2016) and positional behavior (Le Maître et al., 2017), albeit not without criticism (Rae et al., 2016; Benson et al., 2017; Coutier et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Spoor et al., 1994; Spoor et al., 2007; Walker et al., 2008; Silcox et al., 2009; Ryan et al., 2012; Perier et al., 2016.

claim: Differences in the relative size and morphology of the SCs have been correlated with positional behavior.
source: Differences in the relative size and morphology of the SCs have been correlated with locomotor agility (Spoor et al., 1994; Spoor et al., 2007; Walker et al., 2008; Silcox et al., 2009; Ryan et al., 2012; Perier et al., 2016) and positional behavior (Le Maître et al., 2017), albeit not without criticism (Rae et al., 2016; Benson et al., 2017; Coutier et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Le Maître et al., 2017.

claim: The correlation between SC morphology and locomotor agility/positional behavior has been criticized.
source: Differences in the relative size and morphology of the SCs have been correlated with locomotor agility (Spoor et al., 1994; Spoor et al., 2007; Walker et al., 2008; Silcox et al., 2009; Ryan et al., 2012; Perier et al., 2016) and positional behavior (Le Maître et al., 2017), albeit not without criticism (Rae et al., 2016; Benson et al., 2017; Coutier et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rae et al., 2016; Benson et al., 2017; Coutier et al., 2017.

claim: The bony labyrinth morphology has been considered of great importance for phylogenetic reconstruction in various mammals including hominins.
source: On the other hand, the bony labyrinth morphology has been considered of great importance for phylogenetic reconstruction in various mammals including hominins (Quam et al., 2016; Conde-Valverde et al., 2018; Ponce de León et al., 2018; Beaudet, 2019a; Beaudet et al., 2019b) and nonhuman primates (Lebrun et al., 2010; Lebrun et al., 2012; Grohé et al., 2016; Mennecart et al., 2017; Costeur et al., 2018; Schwab et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on hominins and nonhuman primates.

claim: Previous research in hominoids has yielded encouraging results for phylogenetic reconstruction using the bony labyrinth.
source: While previous research in hominoids has yielded encouraging results for phylogenetic reconstruction (Spoor and Zonneveld, 1998; Spoor et al., 2003; Rook et al., 2004; Gunz et al., 2012), according to some authors phylogeny may not be a major component of ape vestibular morphology (Le Maître et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Spoor and Zonneveld, 1998; Spoor et al., 2003; Rook et al., 2004; Gunz et al., 2012.

claim: According to some authors, phylogeny may not be a major component of ape vestibular morphology.
source: While previous research in hominoids has yielded encouraging results for phylogenetic reconstruction (Spoor and Zonneveld, 1998; Spoor et al., 2003; Rook et al., 2004; Gunz et al., 2012), according to some authors phylogeny may not be a major component of ape vestibular morphology (Le Maître et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Le Maître et al., 2017.

claim: A bgPCA performed among major anthropoid groups (platyrrhines, cercopithecoids, hylobatids, and hominids) enables their accurate distinction.
source: A bgPCA performed among major anthropoid groups (platyrrhines, cercopithecoids, hylobatids, and hominids) enables their accurate distinction (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, Figure 2—source data 1), as shown by classification results (more than 95% individuals correctly classified after cross-validation; Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the results of the bgPCA analysis presented in the manuscript, including Figure 2 and Table 1 showing classification accuracy.

claim: More than 95% of individuals were correctly classified after cross-validation in the bgPCA analysis.
source: A bgPCA performed among major anthropoid groups (platyrrhines, cercopithecoids, hylobatids, and hominids) enables their accurate distinction (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, Figure 2—source data 1), as shown by classification results (more than 95% individuals correctly classified after cross-validation; Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the classification results presented in Table 1.

claim: bgPC1 discriminates hylobatids from hominids and all the remaining taxa.
source: In particular, bgPC1 discriminates hylobatids from hominids and all the remaining taxa (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by the bgPCA results shown in Figure 2.

claim: Shape variation in the analyzed sample accounts for a strong phylogenetic signal (Kmult = 1.248, p<0.001).
source: Shape variation in the analyzed sample accounts for a strong phylogenetic signal (Kmult = 1.248, p<0.001), and this also holds for the first three bgPCs separately (see below).
evidence: The claim is supported by the phylogenetic signal analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: bgPC1 (68.8% of total variance) captures differences in thickness and cross-section of the SCs, and is also driven by the development of the macular organs relative to the canals.
source: When analyzed individually, we recover a similarly strong phylogenetic signal (λ = 1 and K = 1.15; Table 2) for bgPC1 (68.8% of total variance). bgPC1 captures differences in thickness and cross-section of the SCs, and is also driven by the development of the macular organs relative to the canals.
evidence: The claim is supported by the bgPCA results and phylogenetic signal analysis presented in the manuscript, including Table 2.

claim: Great apes fall on positive values for bgPC1 due to their stout and flattened SCs combined with an extensive vertical compression of the anterior canal, a more anterosuperior insertion of the lateral canal into the vestibule, and a greater volume of the vestibular recesses relative to the canals.
source: Great apes fall on positive values (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a) due to their stout and flattened SCs combined with an extensive vertical compression of the anterior canal, a more anterosuperior insertion of the lateral canal into the vestibule, and a greater volume of the vestibular recesses relative to the canals (Figures 3a–e, 4a–e and 5a–e).
evidence: The claim is supported by the bgPCA results and morphological observations presented in Figures 2, 3, 4, and 5.

claim: Hylobatids, as well as colobine and papionin cercopithecoids, showing slender and elongated canals but maintaining well developed ampullae, largely overlap on negative values for bgPC1.
source: Hylobatids, as well as colobine and papionin cercopithecoids, showing slender and elongated canals but maintaining well developed ampullae, largely overlap on negative values, while cercopithecins and platyrrhines display intermediate values due to their slightly inflated SCs (Figures 2, 3f–h, 4f–h and 5f–h).
evidence: The claim is supported by the bgPCA results and morphological observations presented in Figures 2, 3, 4, and 5.

claim: bgPC2 (19.6% of total variance) bears strong phylogenetic signal (λ = 0.91; K = 1.51).
source: bgPC2 (19.6% of total variance) also bears strong phylogenetic signal (λ = 0.91; K = 1.51; Table 2), with variance accumulating among rather than within clades (as indicated by K > 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the phylogenetic signal analysis results presented in Table 2.

claim: bgPC2 separates platyrrhines—especially Ateles—from other anthropoids due to the more reduced lateral canal in the former, which is inversely proportional to anterior canal development and vertical elongation.
source: This axis separates platyrrhines—especially Ateles (Figure 1i)—from other anthropoids due to the more reduced lateral canal in the former, which is inversely proportional to anterior canal development and vertical elongation (Figure 2a).
evidence: The claim is supported by the bgPCA results presented in Figure 2a.

claim: Gorilla occupies the opposite end of the distribution for bgPC2 due to its large lateral canal and reduced anterior one, the latter being also vertically compressed.
source: In contrast, Gorilla (Figures 1a, 3a, 4a and 5a) occupies the opposite end of the distribution due to its large lateral canal and reduced anterior one, the latter being also vertically compressed, whereas the remaining hominoids show intermediate values along bgPC2.
evidence: The claim is supported by the bgPCA results and morphological observations presented in Figures 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5.

claim: bgPC3 (11.6% of variance) displays a strong and significant phylogenetic signal (λ = 1 and K = 1.16).
source: bgPC3 (11.6% of variance), which is driven by both trajectory and relative size of the SCs (Figure 2b), still displays a strong and significant phylogenetic signal (λ = 1 and K = 1.16; Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by the phylogenetic signal analysis results presented in Table 2.

claim: Hylobatids display the highest scores for bgPC3, as a result of the right to acute angle formed by the apex of the common crus, a more anterosuperiorly projecting and long anterior canal, an obtuse angle between the planes identified by the anterior and lateral canals, and a more developed lateral canal relative to the posterior one, which is also posteriorly oriented.
source: Hylobatids (Figures 1f–h, 3f–h, 4f–h and 5f–h) display the highest scores for bgPC3, as a result of the right to acute angle formed by the apex of the common crus (CC), the latter being also shorter, a more anterosuperiorly projecting and long anterior canal, an obtuse angle between the planes identified by the anterior and lateral canals, and a more developed lateral canal relative to the posterior one, which is also posteriorly oriented.
evidence: The claim is supported by the bgPCA results and morphological observations presented in Figures 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5.

claim: Oreopithecus (BAC 208) falls on moderately positive scores for bgPC1, where the distributions of hominids, cercopithecins, and platyrrhines overlap.
source: When fossil specimens are plotted a posteriori onto the tangent space identified by extant taxa, Oreopithecus (BAC 208; Figures 1n and 6a) falls on moderately positive scores for bgPC1 (where the distributions of hominids, cercopithecins, and platyrrhines overlap), while the two Australopithecus individuals (StW 573 and StW 578; Figures 1o,p and 6b–c) fall within the range of living great apes and humans (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by the bgPCA results showing the position of Oreopithecus in Figure 2.

claim: The two Australopithecus individuals (StW 573 and StW 578) fall within the range of living great apes and humans for bgPC1.
source: When fossil specimens are plotted a posteriori onto the tangent space identified by extant taxa, Oreopithecus (BAC 208; Figures 1n and 6a) falls on moderately positive scores for bgPC1 (where the distributions of hominids, cercopithecins, and platyrrhines overlap), while the two Australopithecus individuals (StW 573 and StW 578; Figures 1o,p and 6b–c) fall within the range of living great apes and humans (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by the bgPCA results showing the position of Australopithecus specimens in Figure 2.

claim: StW 573 shows more evenly developed canals than StW 578 and BAC 208, which both display a smaller lateral canal.
source: When the relative size of the SCs is taken into account, StW 573 shows more evenly developed canals than StW 578 and BAC 208, which both display a smaller lateral canal.
evidence: The claim is based on morphological observations of the fossil specimens.

claim: StW 573 falls on positive scores for bgPC2, close to the mean value for hominids and cercopithecoids.
source: Their position along the bgPC2 axis reflects these differences, with StW 573 falling on positive scores (close to the mean value for hominids and cercopithecoids; Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1b) and the other two specimens occupying moderately negative values (within the range of extant catarrhines and approaching that of platyrrhines; Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by the bgPCA results showing the position of StW 573 in Figure 2a.

claim: StW 578 and BAC 208 occupy moderately negative values for bgPC2, within the range of extant catarrhines and approaching that of platyrrhines.
source: Their position along the bgPC2 axis reflects these differences, with StW 573 falling on positive scores (close to the mean value for hominids and cercopithecoids; Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1b) and the other two specimens occupying moderately negative values (within the range of extant catarrhines and approaching that of platyrrhines; Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by the bgPCA results showing the position of StW 578 and BAC 208 in Figure 2a.

claim: Oreopithecus falls at the negative end of the extant anthropoid distribution for bgPC3 due to the acute angles between the planes identified by the anterior and lateral canals and that between the planes of the posterior and anterior canals.
source: Due to the acute angles between the planes identified by the anterior and lateral canals and that between the planes of the posterior and anterior canals, Oreopithecus falls at the negative end of the extant anthropoid distribution for the bgPC3 (Figure 2b, Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by the bgPCA results and morphological observations presented in Figure 2b.

claim: The two Australopithecus specimens occupy more intermediate values for bgPC3 because of the possession of a right angle between the planes of the anterior and posterior canals.
source: On the other hand, the two Australopithecus specimens occupy more intermediate values because of the possession of a right angle between the planes of the aforementioned canals.
evidence: The claim is based on morphological observations of the Australopithecus specimens.

claim: StW 573 and 578 fall well within the great ape and human range when the bgPCs are considered at the same time.
source: When the bgPCs are considered at the same time (Figure 2), the australopith specimens fall well within the great ape and human range.
evidence: The claim is supported by the bgPCA results presented in Figure 2.

claim: StW 573 is classified as hominids with p=0.678 based on posterior probabilities of group membership.
source: This is further supported by their posterior probabilities of group membership based on the proximity of fossil specimen scores to groups centroids, with StW 573 and 578 being classified as hominids with p=0.678 and p=0.190, respectively (Table 3).

source: Based on the analysis of the shape of the vestibular apparatus, we identify several potential hominoid synapomorphies (Table 8; Figure 12a–g), including among others a posteromedially displaced posterior canal and a straight segment between the lateral-most point of the lateral canal and its anteromedially situated insertion on the vestibule.
evidence: The claim is based on the morphological analysis and ancestral state reconstructions, with reference to Table 8 and Figure 12.

claim: The anteromedially located lateral canal in hominoids would imply an increased sensitivity for angular accelerations occurring along the coronal plane, which has been correlated with orthogrady in extant hominoids.
source: This would imply an increased sensitivity for angular accelerations occurring along the coronal plane, which has been correlated with orthogrady in extant hominoids (Le Maître et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is an inference about the functional implications of the morphology, with a citation to Le Maître et al., 2017.

claim: The most evident character shared by extant apes and humans is the vertical compression of the anterior canal.
source: The most evident character shared by extant apes and humans (even if somewhat variable in the latter and in Hoolock), and further displayed by the extinct genera analyzed here, is the vertical compression of the anterior canal (Figure 12a), as noted for great apes only in a previous analysis (Spoor and Zonneveld, 1998).
evidence: The claim is based on morphological observations, with a citation to Spoor and Zonneveld, 1998.

claim: The hominoid morphology of the anterior canal might be related to the absence of the subarcuate fossa in great apes and siamangs.
source: Since the subarcuate fossa arguably constrains the shape of the anterior canal (Jeffery et al., 2008), the hominoid morphology might be related to the absence of the fossa in great apes and siamangs (Moyà-Solà and Köhler, 1993; Gannon et al., 1988; Spoor and Leakey, 1996).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis about the relationship between the subarcuate fossa and anterior canal morphology, with citations to supporting studies.

claim: The combination of a well-developed fossa and marked vertical compression of the anterior SC found in Hylobates argues against the hypothesis that the hominoid morphology is related to the absence of the subarcuate fossa.
source: However, the combination of a well-developed fossa and marked vertical compression of the anterior SC found in Hylobates argues against this hypothesis.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on morphological observations of Hylobates.

claim: The cercopithecoid morphology, characterized by a rounded anterior SC even in the largest terrestrial genera, further rejects the hypothesis that the hominoid morphology is related to the absence of the subarcuate fossa.
source: The latter is further rejected by the cercopithecoid morphology, characterized by a rounded anterior SC even in the largest terrestrial genera (Papio, Theropithecus, and Mandrillus), which unlike other cercopithecoids display a much reduced (or even absent) subarcuate fossa (Gannon et al., 1988; Spoor and Leakey, 1996).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on morphological observations of cercopithecoids, with citations to supporting studies.

claim: All hominoids display the anterior canal projected anterosuperiorly to some extent as a result of vertical compression.
source: As a result of vertical compression, all hominoids display the anterior canal projected anterosuperiorly to some extent (less accentuated in Homo and Hoolock).
evidence: The claim is based on morphological observations.

claim: The anterior projection of the anterior canal in Hylobates has been interpreted as a hylobatid synapomorphy.
source: Such a projection of the anterior canal in Hylobates has been interpreted as a hylobatid synapomorphy (Le Maître et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim cites Le Maître et al., 2017 for this interpretation.

claim: The results of this study raise doubts about the view that the anterior projection of the anterior canal is a hylobatid synapomorphy and indicate instead that it is variable within both hylobatids and hominids.
source: Our results raise doubts about the latter view and indicate instead that the anterior projection of this canal is variable within both hylobatids and hominids, and that the LCA of crown hylobatids might have not shown the patent elongation of the anterior canal that is found in Hylobates and Symphalangus.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the morphological analysis and ancestral state reconstructions.

claim: Two potential synapomorphies for hylobatids are an obtuse angle between the planes defined by the anterior and posterior canals, and a posteriorly-inclined posterior canal, which is smaller relative to the anterior and lateral ones.
source: On the other hand, here we identify two potential synapomorphies for hylobatids (Table 8; Figure 12h,i): an obtuse angle between the planes defined by the anterior and posterior canals, and a posteriorly-inclined posterior canal, which is smaller relative to the anterior and lateral ones.
evidence: The claim is based on the morphological analysis and ancestral state reconstructions, with reference to Table 8 and Figure 12.

claim: Hominids differ from other anthropoids, including hylobatids, by derived volumetric proportions of the SCs (stouter canals relative to their length, or shorter canals relative to their volume) even when size-scaling considerations are taken into account.
source: In particular, hominids differ from other anthropoids, including hylobatids, by derived volumetric proportions of the SCs (stouter canals relative to their length, or shorter canals relative to their volume) even when size-scaling considerations are taken into account, as well as by the possession of more extensive vestibular recess for a similar size of the SCs (Table 8; Figure 12j,k), as reflected in bgPC1.
evidence: The claim is based on the morphological analysis and allometry results, with reference to Table 8 and Figure 12.

claim: Hominids possess more extensive vestibular recess for a similar size of the SCs compared to other anthropoids.
source: In particular, hominids differ from other anthropoids, including hylobatids, by derived volumetric proportions of the SCs (stouter canals relative to their length, or shorter canals relative to their volume) even when size-scaling considerations are taken into account, as well as by the possession of more extensive vestibular recess for a similar size of the SCs (Table 8; Figure 12j,k), as reflected in bgPC1.
evidence: The claim is based on the morphological analysis, with reference to Table 8 and Figure 12.

claim: Cercopithecoids and hylobatids completely overlap due to the possession of slender SCs, while hominids differ by their swollen and relatively shorter SCs.
source: In particular, cercopithecoids and hylobatids completely overlap due to the possession of slender SCs, while hominids as a whole (even if more markedly orangutans) differ by their swollen and relatively shorter SCs (with only few cercopithecins falling within the hominid range).
evidence: The claim is based on the morphological analysis and bgPCA results.

claim: The slender SCs of hylobatids and cercopithecoids might be related to the fact that they are swift moving animals that make fast and large head movements, thus requiring a limited duct sensitivity to avoid overstimulation and a quick response to angular displacement.
source: This might be related to the fact that hylobatids and cercopithecoids, unlike great apes, are swift moving animals that make fast and large head movements, thus requiring a limited duct sensitivity to avoid overstimulation and a quick response to angular displacement (Spoor and Zonneveld, 1998).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis about the functional implications of the morphology, with a citation to Spoor and Zonneveld, 1998.

claim: Biophysical models suggest that the length of the membranous ducts is inversely proportional to their sensitivity and that a larger lumen of the ducts correlates with a reduced steadiness of the response to an external angular stimulus.
source: This hypothesis is supported by biophysical models suggesting that the length of the membranous ducts is inversely proportional to their sensitivity and that a larger lumen of the ducts correlates with a reduced steadiness of the response to an external angular stimulus (i.e., the abrupt change of the position and/or posture) (Muller, 1994; Rabbitt et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim cites Muller, 1994 and Rabbitt et al., 2004 for the biophysical models.

claim: Species with shorter and thicker ducts (such as hominids) require more time to perceive and react to sudden head displacements, while being more sensitive to fine movements.
source: Therefore, species with shorter and thicker ducts (such as hominids) require more time to perceive and react to sudden head displacements, while being more sensitive to fine movements.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the biophysical models and morphological observations.

claim: Caution must be used when inferring the lumen of the ducts from that of the bony canals, as the amount of the SC cross-section occupied by perilymphatic space is variable depending on the species.
source: Nevertheless, caution must be used when inferring the lumen of the ducts from that of the bony canals, as the amount of the SC cross-section occupied by perilymphatic space is variable depending on the species (Ramprashad et al., 1984; Spoor and Zonneveld, 1998).
evidence: The claim cites Ramprashad et al., 1984 and Spoor and Zonneveld, 1998 for the variability in perilymphatic space.

claim: There are marked differences among hominid genera in vestibular morphology, mainly relating to the relative size among the SCs.
source: Superimposed on the aforementioned hominoid and hominid synapomorphies (Table 8; Figure 12), there are also marked differences among hominid genera. Such differences mainly relate the relative size among the SCs (which varies particularly along bgPC2 and bgPC3), while hylobatid genera are less diverse in this regard.
evidence: The claim is based on the bgPCA results.

claim: Hylobatid genera are less diverse in vestibular morphology than hominid genera.
source: Superimposed on the aforementioned hominoid and hominid synapomorphies (Table 8; Figure 12), there are also marked differences among hominid genera. Such differences mainly relate the relative size among the SCs (which varies particularly along bgPC2 and bgPC3), while hylobatid genera are less diverse in this regard.
evidence: The claim is based on the bgPCA results.

claim: Chimpanzees and bonobos are characterized by equally developed SCs and a moderately short CC.
source: Chimpanzees and bonobos are characterized by equally developed SCs and a moderately short CC.
evidence: The claim is based on morphological observations.

claim: Orangutans possess evenly proportioned SCs and can be distinguished from Pan by a shorter CC, more inflated canals, and a greater vertical compression of the anterior SC.
source: Similarly, orangutans possess evenly proportioned SCs and can be distinguished from Pan by a shorter CC, more inflated canals, and a greater vertical compression of the anterior SC.
evidence: The claim is based on morphological observations.

claim: Gorillas display the largest intrageneric variability in the studied sample, especially with regard to SCs slenderness, coupled with some other distinctive traits (obtuse angle of the CC apex, and longer lateral SC and CC).
source: Gorillas display the largest intrageneric variability in the studied sample, especially with regard to SCs slenderness, coupled with some other distinctive traits (obtuse angle of the CC apex, and longer lateral SC and CC).
evidence: The claim is based on morphological observations.

claim: Humans differ from apes in the enlarged vertical canals, a laterally protruding and inferiorly displaced posterior canal, and a moderately smaller lateral canal.
source: Humans differ from apes in the enlarged vertical canals, a laterally protruding and inferiorly displaced posterior canal, and a moderately smaller lateral canal.
evidence: The claim is based on morphological observations.

claim: Relatively enlarged vertical canals are also found in Theropithecus.
source: Relatively enlarged vertical canals are also found in Theropithecus.
evidence: The claim is based on morphological observations.

claim: The human morphology of enlarged vertical canals has been linked to bipedalism.
source: The human morphology has been linked to bipedalism (Spoor et al., 1994; Spoor et al., 2003), as accelerations during bipedal walking mainly occur along the vertical axis, so that the broadly similar morphology of Theropithecus might be related to the bipedal shuffling characteristic of this genus during foraging, causing them spend an extremely large amount of time with an erect trunk posture (Wrangham, 1980).
evidence: The claim cites Spoor et al., 1994 and Spoor et al., 2003 for the link to bipedalism.

claim: The broadly similar morphology of Theropithecus might be related to the bipedal shuffling characteristic of this genus during foraging, causing them spend an extremely large amount of time with an erect trunk posture.
source: The human morphology has been linked to bipedalism (Spoor et al., 1994; Spoor et al., 2003), as accelerations during bipedal walking mainly occur along the vertical axis, so that the broadly similar morphology of Theropithecus might be related to the bipedal shuffling characteristic of this genus during foraging, causing them spend an extremely large amount of time with an erect trunk posture (Wrangham, 1980).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis about the functional implications of the morphology, with a citation to Wrangham, 1980.

claim: Vestibular variation bears strong phylogenetic signal and has potential for reconstructing the evolutionary history of hominoids.
source: Irrespective of the functional implications of the variation in vestibular morphology among anthropoids, our analyses show that this variation bears strong phylogenetic signal and, hence, has potential for reconstructing the evolutionary history of the group—particularly hominoids, which in spite of their extant decimated diversity are more variable in this regard (particularly when size differences among the SCs are considered) (Spoor and Zonneveld, 1998; Le Maître et al., 2017) than the taxonomically more diverse cercopithecoids.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the phylogenetic signal analysis results, with citations to Spoor and Zonneveld, 1998 and Le Maître et al., 2017.

claim: Hominoids are more variable in vestibular morphology than the taxonomically more diverse cercopithecoids.
source: Irrespective of the functional implications of the variation in vestibular morphology among anthropoids, our analyses show that this variation bears strong phylogenetic signal and, hence, has potential for reconstructing the evolutionary history of the group—particularly hominoids, which in spite of their extant decimated diversity are more variable in this regard (particularly when size differences among the SCs are considered) (Spoor and Zonneveld, 1998; Le Maître et al., 2017) than the taxonomically more diverse cercopithecoids.
evidence: The claim is based on the morphological analysis results, with citations to Spoor and Zonneveld, 1998 and Le Maître et al., 2017.

claim: To the extent that vestibular morphology appears to be linked to positional behavior, the higher variation of vestibular morphology displayed by hominoids compared to cercopithecoids agrees with the more diverse and varied locomotor repertoires of the former.
source: Therefore, to the extent that vestibular morphology appears to be linked to positional behavior (Spoor et al., 1994; Spoor et al., 2007; Walker et al., 2008; Silcox et al., 2009; Ryan et al., 2012; Le Maître et al., 2017), the higher variation of vestibular morphology displayed by hominoids compared to cercopithecoids agrees with the more diverse and varied locomotor repertoires of the former.
evidence: The claim is an inference about the relationship between vestibular morphology and locomotor diversity, with citations to supporting studies.

claim: Cercopithecoids as a whole are largely pronograde terrestrial quadrupeds that mostly differ in the degree of arboreality vs. terrestriality.
source: This is because cercopithecoids as a whole are largely pronograde terrestrial quadrupeds that mostly differ in the degree of arboreality vs. terrestriality (Fleagle, 2013; Gosselin-Ildari, 2013), while crown hominoids are characterized by a derived and versatile orthograde body plan and associated adaptations throughout the body that enable very different and very specialized antipronograde behaviors—vertical climbing (all apes), ricochetal brachiation (hylobatids), arboreal quadrumanous suspension and clambering (orangutans), below-branch arm-swinging as well as semiterrestrial knuckle-walking (African apes), and terrestrial bipedalism (humans) (Hunt, 1991; Thorpe and Crompton, 2006).
evidence: The claim is a statement about cercopithecoid locomotion, with citations to Fleagle, 2013 and Gosselin-Ildari, 2013.

claim: Crown hominoids are characterized by a derived and versatile orthograde body plan and associated adaptations throughout the body that enable very different and very specialized antipronograde behaviors.
source: This is because cercopithecoids as a whole are largely pronograde terrestrial quadrupeds that mostly differ in the degree of arboreality vs. terrestriality (Fleagle, 2013; Gosselin-Ildari, 2013), while crown hominoids are characterized by a derived and versatile orthograde body plan and associated adaptations throughout the body that enable very different and very specialized antipronograde behaviors—vertical climbing (all apes), ricochetal brachiation (hylobatids), arboreal quadrumanous suspension and clambering (orangutans), below-branch arm-swinging as well as semiterrestrial knuckle-walking (African apes), and terrestrial bipedalism (humans) (Hunt, 1991; Thorpe and Crompton, 2006).
evidence: The claim is a statement about hominoid locomotion, with citations to Hunt, 1991 and Thorpe and Crompton, 2006.

claim: Extant hominoid lineages have more significantly diverged in different directions from their last common ancestor with cercopithecoids in terms of positional behavior, which explains why extant hominoids more strongly differ in vestibular features.
source: The fact that, in terms of positional behavior, extant hominoid lineages have more significantly diverged in different directions from their last common ancestor with cercopithecoids explains why extant hominoids more strongly differ in vestibular features—even if the functional link of some vestibular features remains to be better determined.
evidence: The claim is an inference about the relationship between locomotor diversity and vestibular morphology variation.

claim: Determining the order in which vestibular features evolved is required to use them for inferring the phylogenetic placement of extinct hominoids.
source: Determining the order in which these features evolved is therefore required to use them for inferring the phylogenetic placement of extinct hominoids.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological requirements for phylogenetic inference.

claim: From the LCA of crown hominoids, great apes and humans appear derived in the opposite direction of hylobatids with regard to their volumetric proportions (stout vs. slender SCs, respectively).
source: From the LCA of crown hominoids, great apes and humans appear derived in the opposite direction of hylobatids with regard to their volumetric proportions (stout vs. slender SCs, respectively).
evidence: The claim is based on the ancestral state reconstruction results.

claim: According to the ancestral state reconstruction for crown hominoids, hylobatids appear secondarily convergent with cercopithecoids in terms of SC volumetric proportions.
source: According to our ancestral state reconstruction for crown hominoids, in this regard hylobatids appear secondarily convergent with cercopithecoids.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the ancestral state reconstruction results.

claim: The hypothesis that hylobatids are secondarily convergent with cercopithecoids should be tested by adding extinct stem cercopithecoids and fossil hominoids of less controversial affinities than Oreopithecus to the analysis.
source: However, this hypothesis (and the alternate one, that hylobatids merely reflect more closely the primitive condition for crown catarrhines as a whole) should be tested by means of adding extinct stem cercopithecoids and fossil hominoids of less controversial affinities than Oreopithecus to the analysis.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: Hoolock, in agreement with the basal position of this genus among extant hylobatids, apparently retains a more primitive morphology than other hominoids for various features.
source: It is noteworthy that Hoolock, in agreement with the basal position of this genus among extant hylobatids, apparently retains a more primitive morphology than other hominoids for various features.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the morphological analysis and phylogenetic position of Hoolock.

claim: While the characters related to an anteromedial displacement of the lateral SC appear synapomorphic for hominoids, the only incipient vertical compression of the anterior canal SC morphology of Hoolock might be plesiomorphic for hylobatids.
source: While the characters related to an anteromedial displacement of the lateral SC appear synapomorphic for hominoids, the only incipient vertical compression of the anterior canal SC morphology of Hoolock might be plesiomorphic for hylobatids, in which case the marked vertical compression of this canal would be a synapomorphy of hominids only, with the remaining hylobatid genera having also evolved it in parallel.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis about the evolution of the anterior canal morphology, based on the morphological analysis and ancestral state reconstructions.

claim: Various great ape lineages and humans further diverged from one another from the more derived condition of the reconstructed crown hominoid LCA.
source: While various great ape lineages and humans further diverged from one another from the more derived condition of the reconstructed crown hominoid LCA, as noted above gibbons and siamangs might have secondarily converged to some extent with cercopithecoids by evolving slenderer SCs, presumably as a result of similar evolutionary pressures posed by fast-moving types of locomotion.
evidence: The claim is based on the ancestral state reconstruction results.

claim: Gibbons and siamangs might have secondarily converged to some extent with cercopithecoids by evolving slenderer SCs, presumably as a result of similar evolutionary pressures posed by fast-moving types of locomotion.
source: While various great ape lineages and humans further diverged from one another from the more derived condition of the reconstructed crown hominoid LCA, as noted above gibbons and siamangs might have secondarily converged to some extent with cercopithecoids by evolving slenderer SCs, presumably as a result of similar evolutionary pressures posed by fast-moving types of locomotion.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis about the evolution of hylobatid SC morphology, based on the ancestral state reconstruction results and functional considerations.

claim: Based on the reconstructed ancestral morphotypes, bonobos and (to a lesser extent) chimpanzees would be closer to the LCAs of hominids, hominines, and the Pan-Homo clade, than either humans or the remaining extant great apes (gorillas and orangutans).
source: Based on our reconstructed ancestral morphotypes, bonobos and (to a lesser extent) chimpanzees would be closer to the LCAs of hominids, hominines, and the Pan-Homo clade, than either humans or the remaining extant great apes (gorillas and orangutans).
evidence: The claim is based on the ancestral state reconstruction results.

claim: Gorillas and orangutans would have diverged from the hominid LCA in markedly different directions both in terms of SC configuration and stoutness.
source: The latter would have diverged from the hominid LCA in markedly different directions both in terms of SC configuration and stoutness.
evidence: The claim is based on the ancestral state reconstruction results.

claim: The results support the view that not only hominins, but also gorillas and, to a large extent, the orangutan lineage diverged from ancestors with a largely Pan-like vestibular morphology.
source: Our results therefore support the view that not only hominins, but also gorillas and, to a large extent, the orangutan lineage diverged from ancestors with a largely Pan-like vestibular morphology.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the ancestral state reconstruction results.

claim: Caution is required when interpreting the pattern of vestibular evolution in locomotor terms, as other selection pressures and/or non-adaptive factors could have potentially played an equally, if not more significant, role in determining vestibular shape variation in hominoids.
source: It would be tempting to interpret this pattern in locomotor terms (e.g., by suggesting a semiterrestrial ancestry not only for hominines, but also for crown hominids as a whole). However, caution is required as other selection pressures and/or non-adaptive factors could have potentially played an equally, if not more significant, role in determining vestibular shape variation in this group.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement about the interpretation of the results.

claim: Australopithecus not only displays the various hominoid synapomorphies mentioned above, but also hominid-like volumetric proportions of the SCs and human-like vestibular features such as large anterior and posterior canals.
source: With regard to the fossil hominoids analyzed here, Australopithecus not only displays the various hominoid synapomorphies mentioned above, but also hominid-like volumetric proportions of the SCs and, as expected in a bipedal hominin, human-like vestibular features such as large anterior and posterior canals.
evidence: The claim is based on the morphological analysis of Australopithecus.

claim: The vestibular morphology of Australopithecus is in agreement with the large amount of habitual bipedal behaviors inferred for the almost complete skeleton (StW 573) to which one of the analyzed specimens belongs.
source: This is in agreement with the large amount of habitual bipedal behaviors inferred for the almost complete skeleton (StW 573) to which one of the analyzed specimens belongs (Heaton et al., 2019), as well as previous analyses of the inner ear as a whole (Beaudet et al., 2019b).
evidence: The claim cites Heaton et al., 2019 and Beaudet et al., 2019b for supporting evidence.

claim: Following the ancestral state reconstruction, Australopithecus appears derived in the same direction as humans, although it more closely resembles the morphology of the Australopithecus-Homo clade LCA.
source: Following our ancestral state reconstruction, Australopithecus appears derived in the same direction as humans, although it more closely resembles the morphology of the Australopithecus-Homo clade LCA, which is derived from the reconstructed LCA of the Pan-Homo clade in the opposite direction as chimpanzees and bonobos are.
evidence: The claim is based on the ancestral state reconstruction results.

claim: The fact that the two analyzed specimens of Australopithecus are classified as humans with a moderately high probability reflects the fact that their vestibular morphology already approximates the human condition, although maintaining plesiomorphic characters.
source: The fact that the two analyzed specimens of Australopithecus are classified as humans with a moderately high probability reflects the fact that their vestibular morphology already approximates the human condition, although maintaining plesiomorphic characters, particularly in the specimen that more closely resembles chimpanzees.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the posterior probability analysis results.

claim: The similar classification probability of Australopithecus with other extant great ape genera is consistent with a more primitive vestibular morphology.
source: On the other hand, their similar classification probability with other extant great ape genera is consistent with a more primitive vestibular morphology.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the posterior probability analysis results.

claim: Although the two analyzed individuals of Australopithecus are very similar to one another, they display noticeable differences in vestibular morphology.
source: It is noteworthy that, although the two analyzed individuals are very similar to one another (Beaudet et al., 2019b), they display noticeable differences in vestibular morphology, with StW 578 showing more human-like (even if stouter, approximating the orangutan morphology) canals and StW 573 retaining a more African great ape-like morphology.
evidence: The claim is based on morphological observations, with a citation to Beaudet et al., 2019b.

claim: The differences in vestibular morphology between the two Australopithecus specimens could be related with diachronic changes within South African Australopithecus or to its previously noted heterogeneity.
source: This could be related with diachronic changes within South African Australopithecus or to its previously noted heterogeneity (Clarke, 2013; Grine, 2013), and might help to discern, coupled with other features, the number of species represented among the current samples.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis about the causes of the observed differences, with citations to Clarke, 2013 and Grine, 2013.

claim: Oreopithecus displays a mosaic vestibular morphology that defies a simple phylogenetic interpretation, as it does not fit well among the variation displayed by any extant hominoid genus.
source: Unlike Australopithecus, Oreopithecus displays a mosaic vestibular morphology that defies a simple phylogenetic interpretation, as it does not fit well among the variation displayed by any extant hominoid genus.
evidence: The claim is based on the morphological analysis of Oreopithecus.

claim: Oreopithecus displays a combination of some hominoid and hominid synapomorphies with more plesiomorphic, cercopithecoid-like, or even platyrrhine-like, features.
source: This is due to the combination of some hominoid and hominid synapomorphies with more plesiomorphic, cercopithecoid-like, or even platyrrhine-like, features.
evidence: The claim is based on the morphological analysis of Oreopithecus.

claim: The hominid-like volumetric proportions of the Oreopithecus SCs would support the contention that this taxon is a great ape, or even a member of the European dryopithecine radiation.
source: In particular, the hominid-like volumetric proportions of the Oreopithecus SCs would support the contention that this taxon is a great ape (Begun et al., 1997), or even a member of the European dryopithecine radiation, as previously argued by some authors (Köhler and Moyà-Solà, 1997; Harrison and Rook, 1997).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the morphological analysis, with citations to Begun et al., 1997; Köhler and Moyà-Solà, 1997; Harrison and Rook, 1997.

claim: Other, apparently more plesiomorphic vestibular features of Oreopithecus are at odds with the interpretation that it is a great ape or dryopithecine.
source: However, other, apparently more plesiomorphic vestibular features, are at odds with such an interpretation, and even with the previous suggestion that Oreopithecus postcranium would be consistent with a giant hylobatid that emphasized cautious climbing (Sarmiento, 1987).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the morphological analysis, with a citation to Sarmiento, 1987.

claim: The vestibular morphology of Oreopithecus does not overlap with that of extant hylobatids in any respect, particularly differing by the acute angle between the anterior and posterior canal planes and by the large posterior canal relative to the others.
source: In particular, the vestibular morphology of Oreopithecus does not overlap with that of extant hylobatids in any respect, particularly differing by the acute angle between the anterior and posterior canal planes and by the large posterior canal relative to the others.
evidence: The claim is based on the morphological analysis of Oreopithecus.

claim: Oreopithecus appears more primitive than crown hominoids in the shape of the lateral canal, which is flat (rather than displaying an upwards bent ampullar portion) and posteriorly displaced.
source: Oreopithecus also appears more primitive than crown hominoids in the shape of the lateral canal, which is flat (rather than displaying an upwards bent ampullar portion) and posteriorly displaced (especially in the junction between the ampulla and the vestibular recesses).
evidence: The claim is based on the morphological analysis of Oreopithecus.

claim: In the shape of the lateral canal, the Oreopithecus morphology more closely resembles that of cercopithecoids and platyrrhines, respectively, possibly reflecting a plesiomorphic condition that would be more consistent with a stem hominoid status.
source: In these regard, the Oreopithecus morphology more closely resembles that of cercopithecoids and platyrrhines, respectively, possibly reflecting a plesiomorphic condition that would be more consistent with a stem hominoid status, as recently supported by some other authors (Nengo et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the morphological analysis, with a citation to Nengo et al., 2017.

claim: If the interpretation that Oreopithecus is a stem hominoid is correct, then the stout volumetric proportions of Oreopithecus would be homoplastic with those of great apes and humans, representing an independent acquisition that might be functionally related to the evolution of a slower mode of locomotion.
source: If our interpretation above is correct, then the stout volumetric proportions of Oreopithecus would be homoplastic with those of great apes and humans, representing an independent acquisition that might be functionally related to the evolution of a slower mode of locomotion—in agreement with previous analysis of the inner ear of this taxon (Rook et al., 2004; Ryan et al., 2012) and the possession of an orthograde body plan with adaptations related to cautious vertical climbing and forelimb-dominated suspension (Sarmiento, 1987; Harrison and Rook, 1997).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis about the evolution of Oreopithecus vestibular morphology, with citations to supporting studies.

claim: The hypothesis that the stout volumetric proportions of Oreopithecus are homoplastic with those of great apes and humans is plausible given that hylobatids appear to some extent convergent in this regard to cercopithecoids, due to their agile locomotion.
source: This is plausible given that hylobatids appear to some extent convergent in this regard to cercopithecoids, due to their agile locomotion.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the morphological analysis.

claim: Volumetric proportions of the SCs are quite labile in evolutionary terms, so that other features and functional considerations must also be considered when interpreting the vestibular morphology of extinct taxa in phylogenetic terms.
source: This suggests that volumetric proportions are quite labile in evolutionary terms, so that other features and functional considerations must also be considered when interpreting the vestibular morphology of extinct taxa in phylogenetic terms.
